summary.text: 工 is a whole-graph pictograph interpreted as a tool, though the proposed object is disputed. Today it means work or labor; early uses also include occupations, but the evidence does not establish a clear sequence linking these meanings.

formation.text: Pictographic: early forms are interpreted as a carpenter’s square or another tool, but the precise object is disputed. These accounts treat 工 as one pictured graph, not a combination of separate parts. A transmitted historical explanation instead connects its shape with a person possessing measuring tools and glosses it as 巧飾, skilled finishing; this is a distinct account of the graph.

components.text: 工 is treated as one complete pictorial graph. The proposed referent is a tool, but its precise identity is disputed; no separate internal components are identified.

history.text: Labeled oracle-script and small-seal renderings show historical forms of 工. Early graphs are interpreted as tools, but the proposed object remains disputed. A separate account describes changes in the lower strokes, from a thicker form to a thin horizontal; the sequence does not settle what object the graph depicts.
A transmitted historical account records 𢒄, which includes 彡, as an ancient form of 工. It does not specify whether that graph is an ancestor, a variant, or another kind of related form.

uncertainties.text: The proposed object is disputed, and its spoken name and pronunciation are not established. 工’s reconstructed readings do not identify the object. The cited early artifacts are not dated in the accounts, so they do not establish the earliest attestation of each use.

It is unclear whether early official or status uses relate to craft and work, or whether these meanings form a chronological chain. 工 is also reported as a whole-graph loan for 貢 in oracle-bone contexts; the sound comparison and dates are not established here.

senses.text: The graph is interpreted as picturing a tool, with one account identifying a carpenter’s square. The precise object remains disputed, and the cited accounts do not date the relevant artifacts; this proposal does not establish an attested word meaning or earliest use.
Reported oracle-bone examples use 工 as a state or place name. This use is not connected to the proposed tool meaning.

senses.gloss: official title, status, or occupation term
senses.period: oracle-bone and bronze examples; dating unresolved
senses.text: Reported oracle-bone examples use 工 for status or occupation, including some craft-related uses. A bronze inscription uses it in an official title interpreted as 司空. These title/status and craft-worker uses should remain distinct; their relationship is unresolved.

senses.period: early examples and received Zhouli tradition; dating unresolved
senses.text: Reported examples use 工 for craft workers, including 百工. The received Zhouli tradition also uses it for skilled makers, but these attestations do not date the sense’s beginning or show how it relates to the tool interpretation.
工 currently means work or labor. The evidence does not give a dated sequence showing how these senses developed from the proposed tool or craft-worker senses.

senses.gloss: achievement, written with 工 for 功
senses.period: bronze inscriptions and Warring States bamboo slip; artifact dates unresolved here
senses.text: In cited contexts, 工 is read as 功, ‘achievement’. This is graphic interchange or borrowing in those contexts, not proof that 工’s work sense developed into achievement.

senses.gloss: tribute or offering, written with 工 for 貢
senses.text: In reported oracle-bone contexts, 工 writes 貢. This proposed whole-graph loan means the sign was reused for another word because the words were said to sound alike or similarly, not because the tool meaning changed into ‘tribute’. The early sound match is not independently established by the cited account.

limitations.text: The cited account does not date the artifact examples, so the senses listed here cannot be arranged into a secure chronology. Glosses alone do not demonstrate semantic development.

The proposed tool referent, the relationship between early official or status uses and craft or work uses, and the sound basis of the 貢 loan remain unresolved. Close reconstructed readings for 工, 功, and 攻 do not establish a shared semantic history.
